study.title: 1 Corinthians 15 The Resurrection of Christ and the firmness of Christian Hope
study.overview: Paul responds to the denial of the resurrection of the dead showing that the gospel received by the church includes death, burial, and resurrection of Christ, witnessed by many people. From this truth, he demonstrates that denying the resurrection overthrows one's Christian faith, for Christ raised as the first of the harvest of those who sleep. The chapter culminates in a concrete hope: the dead will be transformed, death will be overcome, and therefore believers must remain firm and active in the work of the Lord.

outline.title: The gospel received and the witnesses of the resurrection
outline.explanation: Paul recalls the central message he preached: Christ died for sins, was buried and rose again, according to the Scriptures. He then presents real witnesses of this resurrection, including Cephas, the twelve, more than five hundred brothers, James, the apostles, and Paul himself, whose life was transformed by grace.

outline.title: The consequences of denying the resurrection
outline.explanation: If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ also did not rise; in this case, preaching, faith, apostolic witness, and hope of the dead would be empty. Paul, however, says the opposite: Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep, and his victory inaugurates the revival of those who are in Christ. The excerpt ends with ethical warnings: bad companies corrupt good customs, and the practical denial of the resurrection leads to permissiveness and spiritual shame.

outline.title: How will the resurrection be: continuity and transformation
outline.explanation: Paul answers the questions about the way of the resurrection by comparing it with the seed: what is planted dies before it sprouts, and God gives the body the form he wants. Thus, the resurrected body will be different in glory, strength and nature: not only the degradable body will be restored, but transformed into a spiritual body, into the image of the heavenly Christ.

outline.title: The final triumph and practical application
outline.explanation: The flesh and blood do not inherit the Kingdom of God in the same way that they are now, so all will be transformed when the trumpet sounds. Death will be defeated, its power attached to sin and the law will be removed, and God will give victory through Jesus Christ. In response, believers must remain firm, immovable and constant in the work of the Lord, because this work is not vain.

study.context: The chapter deals with a real crisis in the Corinthian church: some were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul responds in an orderly manner, first reaffirming the gospel that the church had already received and then showing that the resurrection of Christ is the center of that gospel. The study notes highlight that the problem was serious, because denying the future resurrection also implied denying the resurrection of Christ and thereby emptying the Christian faith. Paul's argument culminates in a pastoral exhortation: the doctrine of the resurrection does not produce speculation, but perseverance, holiness and service.
study.theology: Chapter theology is Christocentric and eschatological. Christ died for sins, rose up bodily and is the first of God's final harvest; his resurrection is a guarantee of the resurrection of those who belong to him. Paul also teaches that mankind is divided between Adam and Christ: in Adam there is death, in Christ there is life. The resurrection is not only a survival of the soul, but the transformation of the body, which passes from corruption to incorruptibility, from weakness to strength, from dishonor to glory. The chapter preserves both personal continuity and real body change. Finally, Christ's victory over death bases an ethics of perseverance, because service to the Lord has eternal value.

scholarViews.insight: The gospel at the center of the chapter is the atoning death and the resurrection of Christ; this truth bases everything that comes next.
Paul uses the resurrection of Christ to refute the denial of the resurrection of the dead, showing that denying one leads to denying the other.
The work of the Lord is to obey his word, and the practical conclusion of the chapter is to persevere firmly in this obedience.

questions: If the resurrection of Christ is historical and central, what in my faith or practice still lives as if this were secondary?
Does my way of serving God show that I believe that work in the Lord is not vain?
What habits, companies or ideas can be weakening my hope in the resurrection and my holiness today?
study.practice: Today, reaffirm the hope of the resurrection with concrete actions: memorize 1 Corinthians 15:58, pray thanking God for the victory in Christ and choosing a practical work of service that you will do without seeking immediate recognition. Also examine whether any company, habit or conversation is producing spiritual cynicism, and change it for communion that strengthens faith and holiness.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail some points mentioned in the chapter, such as baptism by the dead in 15:29 or the fight against beasts in 15:32; therefore, the study only records the general meaning of Paul's argument without filling these questions beyond what the text and notes allow. In addition, Adam Clarke's reference in 15:40 is interpretative and should not be taken as a single definition of the text.
